title: Roles, Users & Privilege Management
description: Architect role-based access control (RBAC), least privilege principles, GRANT/REVOKE, and default privileges.

data.text: In PostgreSQL, users and groups are unified under the concept of **Roles**. A role with the `LOGIN` privilege is equivalent to a user. Best practice dictates creating unprivileged application roles with the minimum privileges required (Principle of Least Privilege).

data.title: Setting up Read-Only and Read-Write Application Roles
data.content: Creating structured roles with automated future default privileges.

data.text: A common production surprise is a role that can `SELECT` from a table but cannot use it because it lacks `USAGE` on the schema containing it, or can insert rows but fails because it has no rights on the identity sequence. Privileges and schema visibility are separate grants, and both must be in place.

data.title: A complete grant for a read/write application role
data.content: USAGE on the schema makes the objects reachable, GRANT on the tables allows the operations, and rights on the sequence allow INSERT to fetch the next id.

data.title: Interview angle: least privilege is a habit, not a grant
data.text: The strong answer is not just 'use GRANT'. It is to separate roles by what they do — an owner role that can run DDL, a read-write application role, and a read-only reporting role — and to make sure the application connects as the least privileged of them. Do not let the application connect as the table owner: owners bypass row-level security, can drop objects, and make an injection bug into a total compromise. `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` is the piece people forget, and forgetting it means every new table silently has the wrong permissions.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Roles represent both individual users and permission groups.
Use `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` so new tables automatically inherit permissions.
Never use the `postgres` superuser for web application connections.
